card.hook: Picture a Venetian street with a painted sky, and not a single gondola traffic jam in sight. That's this corner of The Venetian Macao, a quieter spot than the busy canal bridge, and you'll feel a bit smug finding it.
card.stand_here: Head inside to the 2nd floor and stand on the small bridge beside Lord Stow's Bakery. Face diagonally down the corridor, not straight along it, so the lines lead the eye in.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view down the corridor. Switch to 0.5x if you want more ceiling and the full sweep of the space, but keep the phone level so the lines don't lean.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bright painted sky, then slide it a touch darker so the colours stay rich and the ceiling isn't washed out.
card.best_time: Around 4 PM, when sunlight shines through the painted sky and light falls through the space.
card.selfie_here: Try the overpass in front of The Venetian, with the hotel facade filling the background. Use the front camera at 0.5x, hold the phone a bit low and keep the building over your shoulder. For fewer people, the arched bridge over the main canal just outside St. Mark's Square is worth a go around 9:30-10 AM, before the walkways fill.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the front edge of St. Mark's Square, facing you, while you stand in front of them so the scene behind you fits in.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is not allowed in the ground-floor gaming area, and security will ask you to delete a selfie if gaming tables are in the background. The resort also has shops, a casino and an arena, so check the official site for any access rules before you go.
card.challenge: Shoot a few frames with people walking through and a few without, then pick your cleanest one and see if you can spot the moment the corridor goes quiet.
card.good_to_know: The Venetian Macao is a huge hotel and casino resort on the Cotai Strip, modelled on its sister resort in Las Vegas. The main tower has 39 storeys and the resort opened on 28 August 2007. Inside there are around 300 shops and an indoor canal, and the resort is very large, so allow time to find your way.

card.hook: Picture a 261-metre tower sticking up over a row of ordinary old apartment blocks, like a glass giant who's wandered into the wrong neighbourhood. That's the Grand Lisboa on Rua Nova à Guia, and it's the postcard shot everyone wants.
card.stand_here: Stand on Rua Nova à Guia: from the Grand Lisboa, head north-east to Rua Nova à Guia, about 430 m on foot. Walk on the left-hand pavement and look back towards the south-west to see the tower.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x and let the street lead your eye to the tower. If the top gets chopped off, switch to zoom 0.5x or step back along the pavement. Want the tower bigger above the old buildings? Try zoom 2x or higher, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the tower on one of the vertical lines, then tap the tower and drag the slider to make the picture a touch darker so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning is quieter and the sun is gentler. One guide finds the afternoon light kinder, so try both if you can.
card.selfie_here: Stay on the left-hand side of Rua Nova à Guia and turn around so the Grand Lisboa is directly behind you. Use the front camera, and if you can, hold it a little high. A bollard nearby gives extra height to see the building over the parked cars.
card.ask_someone: Near the Mei Ka Building, with the local market out front, you could ask a passer-by to take your photo, but check on the spot where you can both stand safely on the pavement.
card.rules_and_safety: The street is residential and the traffic is heavy, with many crossings. Stay on the pavement and never step into the road to line up a shot.
card.challenge: Take your shot between passing vehicles, then see if you can get the tower and one old balcony in the same frame.
card.good_to_know: The Grand Lisboa has 47 floors and is the tallest building in Macau. Its casino and restaurants opened in February 2007, and the hotel followed in December 2008. It was designed by Hong Kong architects Dennis Lau and Ng Chun Man.

card.hook: Macau Tower is so tall and slim it looks like someone sharpened a pencil and planted it on the waterfront. The open water in front of it gives you room to step back and fit the whole thing in.
card.stand_here: Stand on the lakeside promenade at Nam Van Lake, a short walk to the north-east of the tower. Face the tower across the water, and hold your phone upright so the full height fits.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the tower, the lake and the skyline together. Try zoom 0.5x for more water and reflection, or zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the tower's shape against the sky.
card.make_it_pop: After dark, switch on night mode, rest your elbows on a railing, tap the tower, then nudge the brightness slider darker so the tower lights don't glare.
card.best_time: Go at sunset or after dark, when the tower and skyline lights are on and the reflections are strongest. Wait for a moment when the water is still.
card.selfie_here: Try the lookout on Penha Hill in front of the Chapel of Our Lady of Penha, where the tower shows up in the distance over the city and lakes. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and check on the spot that the tower sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the street in front of the tower (Rua da Torre de Macau) and shoot upward so the full tower fits, with you in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: Phones are welcome on the main observation decks. For the extreme activities, loose phones typically aren't allowed because they could be dropped. The observation deck and activities are ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the tower standing straight on a gridline with a band of still water along the bottom, and then count how many steps along the promenade it takes to find your favourite angle.
card.good_to_know: Macau Tower stands 338 m high and opened on 19 December 2001. It was inspired by the Sky Tower in Auckland, New Zealand. It sits on land from the Nam Van reclamation project, which added 130 hectares and made the peninsula about 20% bigger.

card.hook: Here's a cheeky trick: at Wynn Macau you get two towers in one photo, the real one and its twin floating in the lake. On a calm evening the reflection is almost perfect.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the whole building and its reflection fit. If the towers get cut off, tap 0.5x and keep your phone level so the edges don't lean. Use 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) for close-ups of the lit facade or a slice of reflection.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the lake edge on the lower third line, then tap the building and slide to darker so the bright lights don't wash out.
card.best_time: Come in the blue hour just after sunset, or at night once the lights are on, when the reflection really stands out. This side is quiet with few people around, and if the water is rippling, wait a moment, because the reflection often sharpens again once it settles.
card.selfie_here: Try the Fortune Fish photo spot at the lakeside gallery of the 'Old Wynn' (that's Wynn Macau, not Wynn Palace), which a guide calls a quirky photo stop. card.rules_and_safety: Flying home from Macau? Selfie sticks over 30cm (retracted) can't go in hand luggage at Macau International Airport. That's a 2019 airport rule, not a hotel or street rule, so check it's still current.
card.challenge: Take three frames in a row and pick the one where the tower and its reflection look most like identical twins.
card.good_to_know: Wynn Macau opened on 6 September 2006. Its second tower, Encore, opened on 21 April 2010, and together they hold 1,008 rooms and suites. If you fancy a different mood, Nam Van Lake Square has a wide lakeside sunset view towards the Macau Tower, but Wynn isn't in that frame.

card.hook: The floor here is the show-off. Black and white waves roll across the square like a calm sea, and every one of them points you at a pastel building.
card.stand_here: Stand in front of the Leal Senado, the cream-white building with green doors and windows, and face it straight on across the square. For the big view, walk to the south end of the square and look along it.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for the Leal Senado front, so the building's lines stay nice and straight. Go to zoom 0.5x to fit the whole square and the wavy floor in one shot. Try zoom 2x or more (higher zooms depend on your phone) for the green doors and windows, or the church in the distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, tap the cream-white wall, then slide it a touch darker so the building keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go early, before about 8 AM, when the square is at its quietest. Weekends and public holidays are very crowded. The December Light Festival and Chinese New Year add extra decorations and colour.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the edge of the central fountain with the colourful buildings behind you. Or try the steps beside the fountain, with the wavy pavement stretching away behind you. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x so more of the square squeezes in. The fountain is sometimes switched off, so don't count on it running.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand at the south entrance and shoot north, while you stand on the wavy pavement near the fountain, so the facades and St. Dominic's Church fit in behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The cobblestone pavement is slightly uneven, so wear comfortable shoes. Around the Leal Senado and the Holy House of Mercy, visitors are asked to stay quiet and respectful.
card.challenge: Find the spot where the wave stripes point straight at the church, then get someone to catch you standing right on the line.
card.good_to_know: Senado Square is part of the UNESCO Historic Centre of Macau. It is named after the Leal Senado, where Chinese and Portuguese met between the 16th and 18th centuries. The wavy Portuguese paving went in during the early 1990s, when the area was closed to traffic. Some walls may have green netting during renovations, so try a tighter zoom or a new angle if one gets in the way.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in front of the Leal Senado, the cream-white building with green doors and windows, and face it straight on across the square. For the big view, walk to the south end of the square and look along it.

card.hook: Here's the surprise: there's nothing behind this front. A whole church burned down in 1835 and only the carved stone face survived, so it stands alone against the sky at the top of 68 steps.
card.stand_here: Stand in Largo da Companhia de Jesus, the square at the foot of the staircase, in the centre. Face the stairs and shoot the whole façade rising above the steps.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole façade and the staircase in one frame. If the square is busy and you can't step back, try zoom 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the carvings and the guardian lions.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, line the façade up with the vertical lines, and hold your phone level so the stonework doesn't lean backwards.
card.best_time: Go early, around 07:30 to 08:30, when the steps and square are less crowded. Light can vary, so have a look on the day.
card.selfie_here: Walk up to Fortaleza do Monte (take the path up on the left side of the ruins) and find the shady spot under the trees. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and keep the façade over your shoulder. One visitor found it quieter than the steps, so it's worth a go.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the lower staircase, right on the centre line of the façade, before about 9 am when the steps are quieter. Ask them to keep the top of the stonework in the frame and use a modest zoom so the whole façade fits.
card.rules_and_safety: You can take photos outside the ruins and in the square in front, but not inside the façade or the museum behind it.
card.challenge: Find the carved seven-headed hydra under Mary's feet, then spot at least one of the six Chinese guardian lions at the base, and get both into your photo roll.
card.good_to_know: The Jesuits built this church and college between 1602 and 1640, and it was among the largest Catholic churches in Asia at the time. A fire during a typhoon on 26 January 1835 destroyed everything except the front. The carvings show the Assumption of Mary, with some Asian touches mixed in. The ruins are part of the Historic Centre of Macau, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Largo da Companhia de Jesus, the square at the foot of the staircase, in the centre. Face the stairs and shoot the whole façade rising above the steps.

card.hook: Picture a bright red gate with green roof edges and stone guardian lions, sitting right against a wooded hillside. That's the first thing you see at A-Ma Temple, and it's a great way to start your photos.
card.stand_here: Stand in Largo do Pagode da Barra (Barra Square, 妈阁前地), the square in front of the temple. Face the red main gate straight across the square and step back a little from it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the gate, the roof edges and the hillside all fit in one frame. Then try 1x for a cleaner look at the gate, and 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the lions and roof ornaments without stepping into anyone's space.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the gate on the centre line with the hillside above it, then tap the gate and drag the slider a touch darker so the red stays rich and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Come between 7 and 9 AM for soft light and fewer people. Sunset light looks lovely on the gate too. The biggest crowds show up during the Tin Hau Festival.
card.selfie_here: Do your selfie at the temple's red main gate, with the gate and wall behind you. One guide calls it a very popular photo spot, because the warm red wall looks great against the hillside. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the gate over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working temple, so be discreet around people praying and don't photograph anyone making offerings or prayers without their okay. Photos outdoors are fine, but one guide says not inside the halls and another allows them before the altars, so check the signs when you arrive. Keep the flash off.
card.challenge: Get the whole gate with a strip of mosaic pavement at the bottom, then find a guardian lion and take a close-up that looks like it's guarding the frame.
card.good_to_know: A-Ma Temple is a working temple to the sea-goddess Mazu, built in 1488, and the name Macau is thought to come from it. It's one of the oldest temples in Macau. It's also part of the Historic Centre of Macau, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2005.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Largo do Pagode da Barra (Barra Square, 妈阁前地), the square in front of the temple. Face the red main gate straight across the square and step back a little from it.

selfie_spots.name: A-Ma Temple Vermilion Main Gate

card.hook: There's a Colosseum on the Macau waterfront, and nobody makes you fight a lion to get the photo. It's a stone-arched replica, big and simple, and it looks great against open sky.
card.stand_here: Head to Macau Fisherman's Wharf, on the Roman-style amphitheatre side near the entrance, outside the arches and columns. Stand about 150 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole amphitheatre in. Go to 0.5x when you're close and want all the arches and steps in one frame, or try 2x-5x from further back for tight shots of the stone columns.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the stone, then drag the slider a little darker so the sky keeps its colour and the stone doesn't look washed out.
card.best_time: Go before or after sunset, when the light is soft and warm on the stone. After dark, switch on night mode and tuck your elbows into your body or lean against a wall to keep still for a few seconds.
card.selfie_here: Use the Amphitheater Photo Spot near the Fisherman's Wharf entrance, on the fenced viewing side in front of the replica. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the amphitheatre over your shoulder, and shoot from outside the fence.
card.rules_and_safety: A fence keeps visitors out of the amphitheatre, so take your photos from outside it. Midday can be hot and some areas have little shade, so carry water in summer.
card.challenge: Take two shots from the same spot: one wide with all the arches and lots of sky, then a close one with just columns and sky. Which one would you frame?
card.good_to_know: Macau Fisherman's Wharf is a themed waterfront complex built in the style of different world seaports, such as Cape Town and Amsterdam. It officially opened on 31 December 2006. The amphitheatre is usually closed because it's a venue for concerts and performances, and many shops and restaurants have been reported closed on some visits, so expect a quiet, open feel.

card.hook: Everyone photographs the Ruins of St. Paul's from the front steps, but up here you get the back of the façade, iron supports and all, with the city spread out behind it. It's the sneaky side view that makes your friends say "wait, where did you take that?"
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, then walk to the south-west battlements of Fortaleza do Monte. Face down the slope and the façade of the Ruins of St. Paul's will be right below you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the big city view. Go to 0.5x for the fort walls and garden, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the façade from the battlements.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the façade, then drag the brightness slider down a touch so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, before about 10am, when the light hits the façade from the east and gives clean shadows. By midday the light is flat.
card.selfie_here: Crouch beside one of the big cannons along the top-level walls, or stand in front of the museum façade with the garden greenery beside you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the fort or the cannon over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Surfaces can be slippery after rain, so wear comfortable shoes and take care on the fort walls. Check the official site for current entrance arrangements, as the museum inside may charge admission and opening times vary.
card.challenge: Crouch beside an old cannon and get it big in the foreground with the Grand Lisboa poking up behind it. Bonus points if the cannon looks like it's aiming at the casino.
card.good_to_know: The fort was built between 1617 and 1626 on a hill about 52 metres high, directly east of the Ruins of St. Paul's, to protect the Jesuits' property from pirates. It helped hold off a Dutch attempt to invade in 1622, and thirty-two cannon were placed around its walls. It opened to the public in 1965 and now houses the Museum of Macau.

card.hook: Picture Senado Square at its busiest: wavy paving, umbrellas bobbing past, a bicycle or two, and one calm yellow church with green shutters waiting at the end of it all. It's the easiest colour-pop photo in Macau.
card.stand_here: Stand in Largo do Senado, on the Senado Square side, and face the church at the top of the square. Let the paving lines run towards the yellow façade.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the church sits inside the square. If the crowds or the width of the square make it hard to fit everything in, drop to 0.5x. Try 2x or 5x for the shutters and white trim (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Tap the façade, then slide the brightness down a touch so the yellow stays rich and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when the square is quieter and your frame is cleanest. The church was reported closed for renovation in late 2024, so scaffolding or barriers may be in the way. Have a look when you arrive.
card.selfie_here: Walk up to St Dominic's Square (Largo de São Domingos) and stand on the wave-pattern paving in front of the church. Use the front camera with the yellow façade over your shoulder. It looks best under blue skies, and you can try 0.5x to fit more of the church in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back toward the far side of the small square in front of the church, while you stand in front of the façade.
card.rules_and_safety: Please stay behind any closure lines, and don't step around one for a cleaner photo. Skip the flash and long photo setups inside the church unless you have permission.
card.challenge: Wait for a bicycle or a bright umbrella to wander through the paving, then catch it leading the eye straight to the yellow church.
card.good_to_know: The Dominican friars finished the church in 1587, but the building you see today dates from the early 17th century, after rebuilding. It's part of the Historic Centre of Macau, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Look for the Chinese-style roof tiles and teak doors, and know that a sacred art museum sits in the bell tower.

card.hook: Imagine a bright white lighthouse and a white chapel standing side by side on the highest hill in Macau, with the whole city and harbour spread out below. It's a ridiculously good backdrop, and you don't need to be a photographer to use it.
card.stand_here: Head to the summit of Guia Hill and stand on the open ground in front of the white walls. Face the lighthouse and chapel so both fit in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the lighthouse, chapel and sky into one shot. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look at the white walls. From the ramparts, try 2x to 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the harbour and far-off buildings.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the lighthouse on one third of the frame with the chapel's white wall beside it, and keep your phone level so the tower stands up straight.
card.best_time: Guides recommend late afternoon or sunset. Some people prefer the morning, so have a look at the sky on the day.
card.selfie_here: Sit on the short wall directly behind the lighthouse, facing out over the view. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and let the lighthouse sit over your shoulder. Few visitors stop there, so you might get it to yourself. For a second option, grab a selfie beside the old cannons next to the lighthouse at the top of the fortress.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Rua Nova da Guia, across from the lighthouse, and shoot you with the lighthouse behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is prohibited inside the Chapel of Our Lady of Guia, so take your pictures outside. The lighthouse is sometimes closed and the cable car doesn't run on Mondays, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Walk over to the ramparts and find the old cannon, then get it, the wide view and Taipa in the distance all in one shot.
card.good_to_know: Guia Hill is the highest point on the Macau peninsula, at about 91 metres. The fort and chapel were built between 1622 and 1638, and the fort was already partly built when the Dutch tried and failed to take Macau. The lighthouse followed in 1864-65 and is described as the first western-style lighthouse on the China coast, and the whole site is part of the UNESCO-listed Historic Centre of Macau.

card.hook: Senado Square is a crowd, but a short walk away there's a quiet square with a fountain, a row of benches and a big Baroque church front. Most people want this shot, and you can usually take your time getting it.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the facade, fountain and benches all fit in. Then go to 1x for a more natural look, and 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for details of the facade.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bright facade, then slide the brightness down a little so the wall keeps its detail.

card.rules_and_safety: The cathedral is an active church. Photography inside is generally allowed, but use no flash, and visitors are discouraged during Sunday services. Check the official site before you go for visiting times.
card.challenge: Get the fountain, the benches and the whole facade in one shot, with nobody walking through (Live Photo helps you pick the cleanest moment).
card.good_to_know: It began as a small wooden chapel in the early 1600s and became a cathedral in 1623. A stone church was consecrated in 1850, but a typhoon almost destroyed it 24 years later. The building you see today was rebuilt in concrete in 1937, and it's part of the Historic Centre of Macau World Heritage Site.

card.hook: You've just fought through the crowds at the Ruins of St. Paul's, and right behind them sits a little grey temple most people walk straight past. It's only 8.4 metres long, so it's easy to miss, and that's part of its charm.
card.stand_here: Stand in Pátio do Espinho, the small courtyard inside the old city wall, reached by the passage beside the temple. Face south-west towards the temple, so the grey roof and stone walls fill the foreground and the old wall rises behind.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the temple, wall and roof together. If the courtyard is too tight to step back, switch to zoom 0.5x, but keep people away from the edges because they get stretched. Try zoom 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for the little ceramic animals along the roof ridge, and hold steady.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the roof line on a horizontal line, and tap the grey wall so it stays crisp. If the sky behind the roof looks washed out, slide it a little darker.
card.best_time: Go whenever the little lanes are quiet, so you can keep people out of the doorway. Spaces here are tight, and fewer people means cleaner frames.
card.selfie_here: Try the tiny Pátio do Espinho lane, entered beside the temple. It's inside the old city wall, and the detailed facades make a good portrait backdrop. Use the front camera, switch to zoom 0.5x if the lane is narrow, and tilt the phone so the wall or temple roof sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Walk down the slope below the temple to where the Grand Lisboa appears in the background, stand there, and ask a passer-by to shoot you from a few steps further down (the temple may not fit in this one).
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working place of worship, so be polite when photographing anyone inside and keep people out of the doorway. Check the official site before you go for current access and visiting rules.
card.challenge: Take three frames of the temple from three heights: low, chest-level and arm's-length overhead. Then pick your favourite and tell nobody about the other two.
card.good_to_know: Na Tcha Temple was built in 1888 and is dedicated to the deity Na Tcha. It's thought to have been raised to help end a plague that was troubling the area. In 2004 it became part of the Historic Centre of Macau, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

card.hook: Picture a yellow church with white trim, two matching bell towers and a stone staircase that practically says "take the photo here." That's St. Lawrence's, and it's one of the tidiest-looking buildings in Macau.
card.stand_here: Stand about 310 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. From there you get a symmetrical, raised view of St. Lawrence's yellow and white facade and both bell towers.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x. If both bell towers won't fit, switch to zoom 0.5x. Down on Rua de São Lourenço, zoom 2x gives you a tighter shot of the facade.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the yellow wall, then slide the picture a touch darker so the white details don't wash out in bright light.
card.best_time: Aim for about 5:00 to 6:30 PM, when the low sun warms the yellow walls. Everything glows.
card.selfie_here: Try the front stone steps on Rua de São Lourenço, with the yellow facade and bell towers behind you. Use the front camera, and switch to 0.5x if the towers won't fit over your shoulder. You can also drop down to the street and face up so the whole church sits behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the opposite side of Rua de São Lourenço, so the full facade and the steps fit in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working church, so keep your voice down, especially during Sunday Mass. Check on site whether photos are allowed inside, and keep the flash off.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines and centre the doorway exactly between the two towers. Bonus points if the palm leaves sneak into the corner of your shot.
card.good_to_know: St. Lawrence's Church (Igreja de São Lourenço) is one of the oldest churches in Macau. The Jesuits first built it before 1560, and it was rebuilt in 1846. It's neoclassical outside, and inside you'll find ornate pillars and chandeliers.

card.hook: Most parks hand you one big lawn and say good luck. Lou Lim Ioc Garden does the opposite: it's a string of little painted-looking scenes, and every turn of the path gives you a fresh one.
card.stand_here: Stand on Nine-Bend Bridge, the zigzag bridge over the lotus pond. Face along its angled sections so they lead the eye across your shot, with the water and greenery around them.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for most views. Switch to 0.5x on tight paths or when you want more of the garden in, and try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out roof edges and carved details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put your main feature on one third of the frame, and let a railing, leaves or a bend in the path sit in front to add depth.
card.best_time: Earlier in the day is usually calmer, with fewer people wandering into your frame. The light under the trees tends to be soft and even, which phones love.
card.selfie_here: Stand at one of the turns on the zigzag bridge over the lotus pond. A local guide says this is where most visitors get their best photo, and each turn gives you a different angle on the water. Or stand in one of the round moon gates with the bamboo grove behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone has it, to fit in more of the scene.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the side or steps of the red pavilion on the small hill, so they can frame the whole garden behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Locals relax here, so be considerate when you're taking photos, especially if anyone might end up in a portrait-style shot. Opening arrangements can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a frame where a leaf or railing sits up close and the garden steps back behind it, then take one portrait-orientation shot and one landscape of the same scene. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: Merchant Lou Kau built the garden in 1906 as part of his residence. Its design follows the well-known gardens of Suzhou, which is why it feels layered rather than open. In 1974 it was handed to the Macau government and became a public park, and local people still use it every day.

card.hook: Picture this: the lake goes still at dusk and Sai Van Bridge suddenly shows up twice, once in the sky and once in the water. That upside-down copy is the reason people gather here.
card.stand_here: Stand in Praça do Lago Sai Van, at the lakeside end near the base of Macau Tower, and face south across the lake. Walk down towards the water's edge so the reflection makes it into your shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the bridge, lake and tower sit nicely together. Try 0.5x for more square and sky, or 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to squeeze Macau Tower and the bridge closer together.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the bridge on the lower third line so the reflection fills the bottom, then tap the bridge and slide it a little darker so the lights don't blow out.
card.best_time: Twilight is the sweet spot. Arrive a little before sunset for a clear daytime shot, then stay while the bridge lights come on and the calm lake reflects them. After dark, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on a railing to keep the phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the lakeside walkway on Sai Van Lake promenade (Avenida Dr. Sun Yat Sen), where the water and bridge are in view across the lake. Use the front camera at 0.5x and turn so the lake and bridge are over your shoulder, and check the preview to see how much of the bridge fits. For a colourful backdrop, the ramp corner near pink-walled Yiwan Alley is a popular photo spot, but its view is Macau Tower, not the bridge.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the square at the foot of Macau Tower, facing the lake and bridge, while you pose a few steps in front of them with the water behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is public, and you don't need a ticket for the view. The Macau Tower observation deck is a separate paid attraction. If you walk the bridge's narrow pedestrian path, remember that vehicles pass by, so stay aware of your surroundings while taking photos.
card.challenge: Can you get a perfectly level horizon with the bridge and its reflection looking like a mirror image? Take three tries and keep your best twin.
card.good_to_know: Sai Van Bridge opened on 19 December 2004 and is about 2.2 kilometres long. It was the third bridge built across the bay between the Macau Peninsula and Taipa Island. Its enclosed lower deck can stay open when strong typhoons close the other two crossings, and it carries the Macau Light Transit System, which began running passengers on 8 December 2023.

card.hook: The pavement in Senado Square looks like frozen waves, and every one of them points you at a calm, plain, very dignified building. Let the floor do the work for you.
card.stand_here: Stand in Largo do Senado near the central fountain, then face south-west. The Leal Senado is to the south-west, about 1 minute on foot, at the end of the square.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole facade and the wavy pavement into one frame. Then try 1x for a calmer, more natural look, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for details like the windows and the entrance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the edge of the pavement on the lower line and keep your phone level, so the waves lead up to the building and the facade doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Go early, before about 10 AM, when the square is least crowded. Weekends and Chinese New Year bring big crowds, so take a few shots in a row while people stroll through.
card.selfie_here: The round fountain in the middle of Senado Square is the classic check-in spot, with the pavement at your feet and the old buildings around you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and check your preview to see how much of the Leal Senado sneaks in behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from in front of the building's white facade, at eye level or low from the side, so the whole building and you are in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The building is a working government office. Photography is restricted in some exhibition areas and the library, so look for signs, and check the official site before you go for interior access.
card.challenge: Get one frame of the wave pavement leading all the way to the facade with not a single stranger in it. Early morning gives you the best chance.
card.good_to_know: Leal Senado means 'Loyal Senate'. Portugal's prince regent gave Macau's government that title in 1810 as a reward for its loyalty. The building went up after 1784 on the site of an earlier Chinese-style pavilion where Portuguese and Chinese officials met. It joined the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2005 and today houses Macau's municipal affairs office.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Largo do Senado near the central fountain, then face south-west. The Leal Senado is to the south-west, about 1 minute on foot, at the end of the square.

selfie_spots.why: A Planchina guide describes this viewpoint as capturing the full sweep of the colonial facades, the wave pavement and the fountain.

card.hook: You puff your way up Penha Hill, turn round, and the pale white chapel and its bell tower are sitting there against the sky like a wedding cake. Then you look the other way and get a second photo for free.
card.stand_here: Stand on Miradouro de Nossa Senhora da Penha, the hilltop platform in front of the Virgin Mary statue, and face the sea. The chapel is just to the north-east, so turn round for it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the statue, sea and skyline in together. Use 1x for the chapel facade, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the Macau Tower closer.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines to keep the horizon level, then tap the bright sky and slide it a little darker so the white chapel keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Late afternoon around golden hour is often recommended for this view. The chapel is white, so it should pick up the warm light nicely.
card.selfie_here: Head to the large open courtyard in front of the chapel and stand beside the marble Our Lady of Lourdes statue. Use the front camera so the open view over Macau fills the frame behind you. The stairs at the chapel's main entrance are another spot to try, with the doorway behind you, but check the angle when you get there.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the broad platform in front of the church, with the Virgin Mary statue at the far end, so the white chapel, bell tower and blue sky all fit in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The hill is steep, so wear comfortable shoes, bring sun protection (the Macau sun is strong) and carry water, as there are no shops nearby. The terrace and outside of the chapel are open, but the inside is often closed or has set hours, so check locally on the day.
card.challenge: Get the statue on one side and the Macau Tower poking up on the other, then take the same shot with the chapel behind you. Two photos, one climb.
card.good_to_know: The first church here was built in 1622 by the crew of the Portuguese ship São Bartholomeu. They had escaped their Dutch pursuers and promised to build a church if they got home safely. It was rebuilt in 1837, then completely rebuilt in 1935 in the Neo-Manueline style, which is the building you see today.

card.hook: The front gate is the obvious shot, but the calmer, prettier picture of the Mandarin's House is round the back, in a small square.
card.stand_here: Stand in Largo do Lilau, the little square behind the house, on the side facing the back of the mansion. Face west and you're looking right at the rear of the house.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the back of the house. If you can't step back far enough to fit the walls in, tap zoom 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) for brickwork, windows and roof edges.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the long wall up along a lower grid line and keep the vertical lines straight.
card.best_time: We don't have a best time for this one. Check the house's visiting days before you go, as entry details can change.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the main gate building (Travessa de António da Silva 10) with the entrance behind you, and use the front camera at zoom 0.5x if your phone has it. For a slower, quieter shot, try the small bridge over the flowing water on the back garden's stone path, with the house behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in Largo do Lilau and aim back at the house, then test the framing together to check the house fits in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography isn't allowed in some areas inside, so check the signs as you go. No flash, and don't touch the furniture. Largo do Lilau is an open public square.
card.challenge: Take three frames from the square, then walk up close and find one brick, door or roof edge worth its own photo.
card.good_to_know: Zheng Wenrui built the house in 1869, and his son Zheng Guanying finished his best-known book, Shengshi Weiyan, here. It covers about 4,000 square metres, which makes it one of the largest family houses in Macau. The style is mostly Cantonese with some western touches, and it joined the UNESCO Historic Centre of Macau in 2005.
